questions.q: Why does reading orders[40000] take the same time as reading orders[0]?
questions.explain: Contiguous storage means one multiplication and one addition find any slot. Nothing walks past the earlier items, so indexing is O(1).
options: The engine caches every index the first time the array is created
The slots are contiguous and equal-sized, so the address is computed directly: start + index × slot size
Arrays are hash maps, and hash maps are always O(1)
It does not; later indexes are slower because the engine counts from 0

questions.q: A "recently viewed products" list adds each new product with unshift. What does each unshift cost on a list of n products?
questions.explain: The slots must stay contiguous from index 0, so inserting at the front moves everything. Adding at the end with push and reading the list backwards avoids the moves.
options: O(n): every existing product moves one slot to the right

questions.q: This loop is meant to remove every cancelled order. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: splice shifts later items left, but i still increases. The skipped item is only checked if you walk backwards or rebuild the array. It is also O(n²) in moves.
options: It throws, because you cannot change an array inside a loop
After a removal the next order slides into index i, and the loop skips it, so two cancelled orders in a row leave one behind
Nothing, it is correct and O(n)

questions.q: Walking the same splice loop backwards (from the last index to 0) fixes the skipped items. What is its cost for n orders when a third of them are cancelled?
questions.explain: Walking backwards fixes correctness, not cost. Removing near the front still moves almost everything behind it. filter or a read/write index compaction is O(n).
options: O(n), because each order is visited once
O(n²) in the worst case, because each splice still moves every item after the removed one
O(1) per removal, because it works from the end

questions.q: You must remove all cancelled orders from 200,000 orders and nothing else holds a reference to the array. Which approach is both correct and O(n)?
questions.explain: filter reads each order once and writes survivors into a new array. The indexOf loop is the worst of all: each search is O(n) and each splice is O(n), repeated for every cancelled order.
options: A while loop that calls indexOf and splice until nothing is found

questions.q: What happens when you write ids[1000000] = "ORD-1" into an empty array?
questions.explain: Holes are missing entries, not undefined values (0 in ids is false). Engines keep fast contiguous storage for dense arrays; very sparse ones may fall back to a dictionary. Keep arrays dense.
options: The engine fills indexes 0 to 999,999 with undefined values in a contiguous block
length becomes 1,000,001 with one real item and a million holes, and the engine may switch the array to slower dictionary-like storage
The item is stored at index 0

questions.q: A payout job empties an array of 50,000 transfers with while (transfers.length) process(transfers.shift()). What is the better way when the array does not need to shrink as you go?
questions.explain: shift and splice(0, 1) both move every remaining item: O(n) each, O(n²) for the loop. An index does not move anything. For a real queue that also receives new items, use a queue structure.
options: Walk an index forward: for (let i = 0; i < transfers.length; i++), which is O(1) per item
Call shift() twice per iteration to halve the loop count

questions.q: You timed shift() on a 100-item array and it looked instant. Why should you still treat it as O(n)?
questions.explain: An engine optimisation is not a guarantee. A test on 100 items hides the growth; measure at production sizes, and design for the documented cost.
options: The specification moves every item; V8 has a trick that avoids the moves for some arrays, but it does not hold for large arrays, and the cost comes back exactly when the data grows
Because shift is O(n²) for every single call
Because small arrays are stored as strings

questions.q: What does currency.toUpperCase() do to const currency = "ngn"?
questions.explain: Strings are immutable. Every method that seems to change one returns a new string, in O(length) time. const is not the reason: a let string would not change either unless you assign the result back.
options: Returns a new string "NGN" and leaves currency as "ngn"

questions.q: What does line.slice(0, 20) cost, and why?
questions.explain: Treat string operations that produce a new string as proportional to the length they produce or scan. Engines sometimes share memory internally, but you cannot rely on it, and the result is still a new immutable string.
options: O(1), because slicing only records two indexes
O(length of the result): a new string is created and its characters are copied

questions.q: Which statement-building loop has a hidden quadratic cost in V8?
questions.explain: V8 makes appending cheap by building a rope and copying later. Reading the partly built string (endsWith, includes, indexing) forces a flatten, a full copy, on every iteration: O(n²) overall.
options: for (const line of lines) { if (!text.endsWith("\n")) text += "\n"; text += line; }
const parts = []; for (const line of lines) parts.push(line); const text = parts.join("\n");

questions.q: Why is parts.join("") a safe way to build a big string on every engine?
questions.explain: The expensive part of repeated concatenation is copying the growing result again and again. join copies each character exactly once.
options: Because join runs in parallel on several cores
It can compute the total length first, allocate the result once and copy each piece once: O(total length)
Because arrays are faster than strings in every situation
Because join does not create a new string

questions.q: Why is "₦".length 1 but "🎉".length 2?
questions.explain: JavaScript strings are sequences of 16-bit code units. Characters outside the first 65,536 code points take two. [...text].length counts code points instead.
options: Emoji are stored as two characters on purpose so that they look bigger
length counts UTF-16 code units; the naira sign fits in one, the emoji needs two (a surrogate pair)
It is a bug in JavaScript that will be fixed

questions.q: Why does text.split("").reverse().join("") break an emoji?
questions.explain: Split by code point with [...text] to keep each emoji whole. Emoji built from several code points (flags, families) need Intl.Segmenter.
options: Because reverse does not work on strings
split("") cuts the emoji into its two surrogate code units, and reversing puts them in the wrong order, which is not a valid character

questions.q: After normalizing the text into an array of code points, a palindrome check compares clean[left] with clean[right] while moving both indexes inwards. What extra space does the comparison itself use?
questions.explain: The comparison only keeps two indexes. The normalization before it costs O(n) space, so the whole function is O(n) space, but the comparison step adds nothing that grows.

questions.q: Checking two voucher codes for anagrams by sorting both and comparing: what is the time complexity for codes of length n?
questions.explain: The sorts dominate. Counting characters with a Map brings it down to O(n), which the hash maps lesson explains.
options: O(n log n), because of the sort

questions.q: A developer checks anagrams with new Set(a) and new Set(b), and returns true when the sets contain the same characters and the lengths match. Which pair shows the bug?
questions.explain: Both contain exactly a and b and have length 3, but the counts differ. A set forgets how many times each character appears; a count does not.

questions.q: Why does rotate compute ((k % n) + n) % n instead of just k % n?
questions.explain: % in JavaScript keeps the sign of the left operand. The empty array still needs its own check first, because k % 0 is NaN.
options: In JavaScript -1 % 5 is -1; adding n and taking % n again turns any negative k into the equivalent right rotation between 0 and n - 1
Because % does not work on large numbers

questions.q: What does rotating by k with k repetitions of items.unshift(items.pop()) cost?
questions.explain: pop is O(1), but unshift is O(n). With two slices or three reversals the cost is O(n) whatever k is (after normalizing k below n).
options: O(n · k): each unshift moves every item

questions.q: Rotating in place with three reversals (whole array, then the first k, then the rest) uses how much extra space?
questions.explain: Every reversal swaps items inside the same array using two indexes. The two-slice version is simpler but allocates a new array: O(n) extra space.

questions.q: You want to store a million balances in kobo in an Int32Array. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Typed arrays store raw numbers contiguously and are fast, but each element type has a fixed range. Float64Array or BigInt64Array fits larger amounts; choose based on the range you need.
options: Typed arrays cannot hold a million items
An Int32Array only holds up to 2,147,483,647, about ₦21 million in kobo; bigger balances silently wrap around
Typed arrays are slower than normal arrays for numbers

questions.q: Inside a loop over 10,000 orders, code calls orders.toSorted(byDate)[0] to find the oldest order each time. What is the problem?
questions.explain: The non-mutating methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with) are safer but always copy. Hoist them out of loops.
options: Each call copies and sorts the whole array, O(n log n), so the loop is O(n² log n); compute the oldest once, or track it in one pass

questions.q: Which test case would have caught the forward splice bug in the cancelled-orders loop?
questions.explain: The bug only shows when the item that slides into the current index also needs removing. Adjacent matches belong in every checklist for loops that remove items.
options: A list with one paid order
Two cancelled orders next to each other
A list where no order is cancelled

questions.q: Write removeCancelled(orders) that returns a new array without the cancelled orders, in O(n), without splice.
questions.explain: filter visits each order once and never shifts anything, so adjacent cancelled orders are handled and the cost is O(n) time, O(n) space for the new array.

questions.q: Remove every out-of-stock product (stock === 0) in place, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, using a read index and a write index. Then truncate the array.
questions.explain: Every kept product is copied once to the write position, and nothing ever shifts. Setting length removes the leftover slots at the end.

questions.q: Write isPalindrome(text) that ignores case and anything that is not a letter or digit, and compares from both ends inwards.
questions.explain: Normalize once (O(n)), then compare pairs until the indexes meet. The empty string has no pair to compare, so the loop never runs and the answer is true.

questions.q: Write isAnagram(a, b) in O(n) time by counting characters with a Map. Ignore case.
questions.explain: Count the first string up, count the second down; a missing or exhausted character means not an anagram. With equal lengths, never going below zero implies all counts end at zero.

questions.q: Write rotate(items, k) that returns a new array rotated right by k. It must handle k larger than the length, negative k and the empty array.
questions.explain: Normalize k into 0 to n - 1, then join the last shift items with the rest. O(n) time and space. Check n === 0 before using %.

questions.q: Build a bank statement with one line per transaction in the form ID amount, using an array of lines and a single join. Amounts are in kobo; print them in naira with two decimals.
questions.explain: Collect the pieces, then join once: every character is copied once, so the cost is O(total length) on every engine, even for a million lines.

questions.q: Write reverseText(text) that reverses by code point, so the emoji survives.
questions.explain: Spreading a string iterates by code point, keeping surrogate pairs together. split("") would split the emoji into two invalid halves.

questions.q: Write removeAt(items, index) without splice: move every later item one place left, shrink the array by one, and return the removed item.
questions.explain: Moving left starts at the removed index and goes forwards (the opposite of inserting). It moves length - index - 1 items: O(n) at the front, O(1) at the end.
